speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: DECLARATION OF LOYALTY ON CELEBRATION OF BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the day
officially appointed for the celebration of the birthday of Her Gracious Majesty the Queen of Canada, Elizabeth II. During the commonwealth prime ministers' conference I had the honour and pleasure of an audience with Her Majesty, and at that time she again impressed me with the warmth of her interest in Canada and the Canadian people. It is, therefore, a special pleasure for me to suggest that the house do reaffirm its loyalty and affection to Her Majesty.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I propose that after the Leader of the Opposition and any other hon. members who desire to participate join me in this tribute, we should stand and sing "God Save the Queen" as an expression of the feelings of her members of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DECLARATION OF LOYALTY ON CELEBRATION OF BIRTHDAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to associate my party and myself with what the Prime Minister has just said. This is a day that gives us an opportunity to reaffirm our respect for the monarchy as an institution which has meant so much to our freedom and development, and our affection and admiration for the person of the monarch herself.

subtopic: DECLARATION OF LOYALTY ON CELEBRATION OF BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group I join the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition in the remarks that have been made by both hon. members with respect to our loyalty to Her Majesty and the great part she plays as Head of the commonwealth.
However I wish to make one suggestion. We would like the Prime Minister to give consideration to the House of Commons showing its delight with this occasion and other national holidays by arranging holidays next year for the members of the House of Commons and the staff. I think that would be most appropriate. I am not in favour of the present habit into which we have fallen.
Whereupon the members of the house rose and sang

should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance; but before so doing, if you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, as a freshman in the parliamentary class of 1945 along with the hon. gentleman, I want to extend to him this group's greetings and best wishes. My question is this. In view of the fact that a Progressive Conservative candidate for the next federal election has stated that in Canada the dollar should be known as "the beaver" and that this change would benefit the tourist business, will the minister inform the house whether the government is giving consideration to such a change? speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):

subtopic: SUGGESTED CHANGE IN NAME OF CANADIAN DOLLAR

First, Mr. Speaker, may I thank the hon. member for his kindly remembrance, which I greatly appreciate. So far as the government's intention is concerned, may I say that the government is giving thought to no such change as is proposed here.
I fancy that the reference in the final part of the question may have been lost on the younger members of the house, but having regard to the historic lore displayed by the hon. member in asking this question I think I should assure him that perhaps he and I could both profit by resort to the beaver as a head-saving and not merely a face-saving device.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Prime Minister gave the house his interpretation of the critical events which were evolving at that time, more particularly out of the failure of the great powers to sit in at what is called a summit meeting in the hope, which was shared by all of us, that such a meeting might have brought about an easing in international tensions.
The statement made by the Prime Minister in which he gave his interpretation of these events was warmly supported by every member of this house. Indeed, on that occasion we witnessed a unanimity of opinion and support not witnessed in this house since the present government took over the reins of office.
One regrets that in respect of current matters of a domestic character it is not possible to find any manifestation of anything like that measure of support. Particularly in so far as our domestic problems affect the maintenance of a high and stable level of income, there is no solid agreement except among those who sit on the treasury benches, supported by those sitting behind the ministers of the crown.
It would seem that at this time of disquietude in our country it is becoming gradually and increasingly acknowledged in this house and in this country that through the present government there is a want of


leadership which reflects itself in the character of our economic policies. I do not say there is no leadership, but the leadership does not come from the government of the day. The lack of leadership is demonstrated not only in the person of the right hon. gentleman who is the Queen's first minister, but it touches other departments of government. Certainly it touches the Department of Finance (Mr. Fleming) over which presides the present minister-an old friend, a classmate whom I am happy to congratulate today on his surprisingly young fifty fifth birthday.
It touches as well, of course, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and his department; it is not unrelated to the administration of national defence as reflected in the uncertain policy on defence that we have in this country. I cannot say that the demonstrations or the manifestations of lack of affinity in the case of the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) are as apparent as they are in some other departments, but I will say to the Solicitor General that there are occasions-those few occasions when he speaks in this house-when one is not altogether confident about the kind of leadership he himself gives to the very weighty department of government for which he has the responsibility of administration.
As to the Department of Transport there are, of course, indications there too. In agriculture, having in mind the depressed state which prevails in this very important section of the Canadian economy, and having in mind the changes in policy that have been pursued by the minister in respect of his administration, I suppose we would not find it very difficult to suggest that the kind of leadership which the Canadian farmer expects has not been coming from him.
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), who is a new minister and also an old friend, will not mind my saying about him and his administration that the unsatisfactory state of the government's housing policy is not such as to warrant any real feeling of confidence on the part of the Canadian people. I have already indicated on other occasions to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) that the growing problem of unemployment in Canada is not such as to warrant a comfortable feeling, in so far as his department is concerned, or that the situation has been handled in accordance with commitments made by the administration. In his case I recognize at once, however, that the responsibility is so great that in all fairness it should be shared by the government as a whole.

Nevertheless it cannot be questioned that in respect of economic matters in this country, matters affecting our trade with other countries, the increasing level of imports, the growing problem of unemployment or the high level of unemployment, and the present state of the national income, the one single voice giving leadership in this country at the present time is not that of the government of the day but that of the governor of the Bank of Canada. That, in a democracy such as our own, is a serious reflection on the efficiency of the government.
The governor of the Bank of Canada has not been afraid to assess economic realities, actual and potential, as he sees them. He has regarded this assessment as part of his function. But his assessment has been accompanied by a tempered optimism as to the capacity of our people to meet the problems which now exist and those which lie ahead. In a memorable speech on May 12, at Hamilton, the governor of the Bank of Canada said, in the opening part of his statement:
I shall probably not make myself popular by remarking that all is not gold that glitters. It is not a pleasant task to talk about economic problems rather than successes, about difficulties and dangers rather than achievements and enjoyments, yet I suppose that at times this must be the function and the duty of a central banker. If we do not see the dangers and pay heed to them, we shall never reach the goal that shines so invitingly.
I am sure that no one knowing the responsibility of the Bank of Canada to parliament will fail to appreciate the honesty of this kind of approach to our problems. It will be charged, undoubtedly, that those in the opposition are guilty of preaching gloom throughout the country; that we are harbingers of doom and gloom-

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen say hear, hear. All I can say is that we are in good company; we are in the company of the governor of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: No, you are not.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
If the government of the day feels that the governor of the Bank of Canada is not expressing its views, there are constitutional processes to which the government of the day can easily resort to remove any inconsistency in the administration of the Bank of Canada, or remove from any responsible office in that important institution, responsible to this parliament, those who express views on which the government of the day does not rely or in which it does not believe.
But the governor of the Bank of Canada is not alone in this position. He is supported by important public officials in the public
National Board on Economic Development service of Canada who serve this government and who serve the people; and I suggest that while the governor of the Bank of Canada was undertaking a series of important speeches in different parts of Canada, almost at the same time the Minister of Finance was making speeches in Vancouver and in Winnipeg. The difference in the tone and in the direction of those two speeches indicates that the Minister of Finance certainly does not fully share the point of view expressed by the governor of the Bank of Canada in the speech made on May 12 in Hamilton. If he does, he will have an opportunity to say so. Certainly the speeches made by him in this house in answer to that made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) during the budget debate, the speeches made by the Minister of Finance in the two cities to which I made reference a moment ago, do not support the view that he shares the concerns and the solutions of the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Therefore no one in the opposition can be said to have met his responsibility if in assessing our problems he does not make the same straightforward, courageous assessment, also providing at the same time his proposals as to what may be the remedies.
We will not correct the dangers which seem to be lurking ahead unless we know what those dangers are, and unless we are prepared to take courageous steps to meet them.
Our objective in this country must be to maintain a high and stable level of income, and to provide jobs for our people. No other objective will be worthy of our society. That is the objective as stated by the governor of the Bank of Canada. At pages 15 and 16 of the text of his speech, released by him, he said:
We can have economic growth without inflation, full employment without inflation, a rising standard of living without inflation, increased social services in various forms of government services without inflation, and a balance in our international accounts without inflation-and without unemployment. All this is within our own power to achieve.
That ought to be, if it is not, the objective of the government of this country. The government will find that the difficult situation which confronts us is actually a situation which well-known, knowledgeable individuals, who by training are in a position to comment on these matters, have indicated may confront us. The precedent to which I direct the attention of the government will be found in the white paper issued by the government of Canada prior to the end of the second world war, when the great concern was what kind of transition would be made from war to peace. It was suggested, and by many members in the house at that time, that once the
4130	HOUSE OF
National Board on Economic Development war was over there would be a drop in the national income and we would see a repetition of the unemployment of the dark 1930's.
We know that after the war Canada enjoyed the most prosperous period in her history, with more men in the working force, more employment, a higher national income both in terms of the nation and of the individual citizen, than ever before; all during the period when our growing prestige among the nations of the world was widely recognized.
How was that achieved? It was achieved because the government of the day recognized that there were dangers ahead; that with the cessation of war there would be problems that would touch every department of government, as well as the citizens of this country. I examined the situation in anticipation, and it stated its objectives in the white paper, a copy of which I now have in my hand. This white paper is something for the government to look at now, in the face of the economic problems that confront Canada. In the fourth paragraph of that statement the government said:
The central task of reconstruction, In the interest of the armed services and civilians alike, must be to accomplish a smooth, orderly transition from the economic conditions of war to those of peace and to maintain a high and stable level of employment and income. The government adopts this as a primary object of policy.
Have we heard from this government since the last election any declaration of an objective in these bold terms? The government went on to point out in this white paper:
This goal cannot be achieved by legislation alone, nor by a single device or plan. In this, it is like the wartime stabilization program. Its attainment will require the effective working of a number of compatible policies, all directed to the same end, and each contributing to the success of the others.
Then at page 3 of this white paper will be found the plans which the government was going to follow to channel manpower and resources after the war was over in directions that would contribute to the economic enhancement of this nation and its people. Those purposes were carefully followed and the consequence was that the government, in co-operation with the people of Canada, was able to build up a high standard of living at the end of the most cataclysmic experience in the history of mankind instead of allowing to happen what followed in this and other countries at the conclusion of the first world war. The government said in the summary of its conclusions:
In this paper, the government has stated unequivocally its adoption of a high and stable level of employment and income, and thereby higher standards of living, as a major aim of government policy. It has been made clear that, if it is to be achieved, the endeavour to achieve it must pervade


all government economic policy. It must be wholeheartedly accepted by all economic groups and organizations as a great national objective, transcending in importance all section and group interests.
That statement is not unlike the words of the governor of the Bank of Canada, who enlisted the direction of the senior government and the other levels of government in co-operation with all groups in the nation in trying to meet the current economic problem and to arrest or deal with other economic dangers which he said lie ahead in the next ensuing period for this country. Have we had from this administration that kind of approach? We have not had from the Minister of Finance, from the Prime Minister or from any of their colleagues any indication that they look upon the problem as requiring this bold approach.
It cannot be because the government has not been advised by its own servants, perhaps the foremost among whom, next to the governor of the Bank of Canada, is Dr. Firestone, who confronted the government last October with an important statement in which he said, looking ahead to the immediate future:
-we can see a fair rate of increase in economic activity for 1960 and possibly 1961... If anything, the problems that we may be encountering as we go into 1962 may be more difficult to deal with than those we encountered in the post-war period. What I am implying is that the recession we may be facing in 1962 could be more extensive than anything we have yet experienced since the end of world war II-
It is true that the prognostication of this distinguished public servant does not, in so far as timing is concerned, harmonize with the observations made by the governor of the Bank of Canada or by certain other economic authorities in the country. But that was last October. There has been an acceleration of events noted by economic specialists which undoubtedly would warrant Dr. Firestone in timing his prognosis in accordance with events as they now confront us, and as seemingly they begin now to indicate an earlier arrival than was formerly the case.
But we do not only have the observations of those to whom I have already made reference. We have the observations of General Research Associates, directed by a gentleman who was at one time in the government service occupying a very important assistant post in the prosecution of economic studies involving forecasts and suggested remedies. I refer to such statements made in January of 1960, March of 1960 and April, 1960 all in the same vein. I now have before me the latest monthly business forecast of General Research Associates, whose references in the months of January, March and

April I have already alluded to. In the first paragraph on page 2 of this report there is this observation:
The leading business indicators as a group continue to reveal recession tendencies. Industrial common stock prices have moved seasonally and irregularly for the past four months, an indication of continued uncertainty.
Then in the fifth paragraph this is noted:
The pattern of the leaders as a group is one which precedes by no more than a few months significant declines in production, employment and other central measures of over-all Canadian business activity.
If this particular organization, General Research Associates, is to be given the respect and attention which it receives from most students of this situation, we have a right to ask the government whether it agrees with these danger signals it has pointed out, or whether the government has a different position. We have the right to ask, will the government tell us what its own private confidential reports indicate. Some of these reports the government has not hesitated to make public. One that was always regarded as confidential was trotted out on the floor of the house by the Prime Minister in 1958. It would be interesting to know from the Minister of Trade and Commerce what that so-called secret report indicates. What does the "Economic Outlook for 1960" indicate? Does it confirm the judgment of the governor of the Bank of Canada? Does it confirm the view of the gentlemen associated with General Research Associates?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order. This is a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply. On such a motion it is open to any hon. member, of course, to rise to air a grievance; and if he has, as the hon. member for Essex East has, the opportunity of leading the debate, to introduce an amendment to express his view with respect to the grievance. But there must be a grievance. Otherwise, in my submission the type of discussion that is evidently being embarked upon is, it seems to me, quite apart from the course that is required by the rules in such situations.
What we have had so far has just been a repetition of the kind of speeches that were made by the hon. member and the Leader of the Opposition in the budget debate. Apparently we are just having a repetition of such speeches on this occasion. With great respect, Mr. Speaker, that is quite out of order at this stage of the session. All these matters that have been mentioned so far were raised in speeches made in the budget debate. If the hon. member says this is just his introduction to his grievance, then with
National Board on Economic Development respect he has gone the long way around. Mr. Beckett was asked':
Will the next recession be the worst since the thirties?
His answer was:
I would say yes. Definitely.
Then he went on to point out that this is the result of having too rapid an expansion of capital goods for too long, over a period of 10 years. Then when he was asked about unemployment in terms of this particular situation he said:
I foresee it reaching 1.5 million.
This statement was not made during the budget debate but appeared in written form in Maclean's magazine, the issue of June 4. Further questions were proposed, and he said this about the situation:
It could be softened by a vast increase in government spending at all levels-including city redevelopment, new schools, highways, hospitals and houses.
The minister, or whoever replies for the government, will, I trust, address himself to this particular question and answer this distinguished economist. Are these facts correct? Does the government support the positions taken by these gentlemen? Does the government agree with the conclusion reached in the last issue of the bulletin put out by the congress of labour which says, on page 7:
Unless we run into some quite extraordinary good fortune or unless the government adopts some drastically new policies, we shall still this summer and fall have unemployment much heavier than in most post-war years, very much heavier than in the best post-war years.
Are these indications from these various sources true? What does the confidential document, which when I was in the Department of Labour was presented' to the minister twice a year, indicate as to the possibility of improving the present unemployment picture this summer? What are the prognostications for next fall and next winter? Are these not matters to which this house should be prepared to give its full attention? Are these matters not questions to which we have a right to ask the government to give us clear answers? Can there be any doubt as to the situation that confronts us in terms of the maintenance of a high and stable level of income? Is the situation not reflected in the


general economic conditions that prevail in the country, in the very high level of unemployment that continues to persist?
When we look at the current economic conditions, is it possible for anyone not to be concerned? There are still, of course, elements of strength. Our exports reveal that to be the case. These have been maintained at a high level during the first quarter of 1960, and we hope this trend will be maintained. But will they be maintained in the face of the new trading relations in Europe and the lack of a dynamic trade policy in Canada?
What about the agricultural sector of our economy? It is going through, admittedly, a new and difficult period. We note that in 1959 farm net income declined by more than 7 per cent, according to the Department of Agriculture. It will show a further reduction in 1960. Retail sales, which are considered to be a very good indicator of the rate of economic activity, have not shown any material increase in the first quarter of 1960 as compared with the first quarter of 1959. The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin, issue of May 20, indicates that these sales have increased by about $8 million in the first quarter of this year as compared with last year, which in percentage terms is less than three tenths of one per cent.
Another sign of economic inactivity or of serious weakness in the economy is to be found in the field of housing. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, starts in construction of new residential units in the first quarter fell to 11,118 from 16,365 a year earlier. This represents a decline of 35 per cent. The impact of this decline is not limited to the construction industry. It is felt in industries supplying construction materials, and in numerous other industries producing durable consumer goods like furniture and electronic appliances. Moreover, the bureau of statistics, in its weekly bulletin of Friday, May 13, 1960 points out that the output of motor vehicles declined to 42,000 from 44,659 in the same month last year.
Another significant indicator of activity is Canada's railway systems. Here again there are elements of weakness portrayed. According to this bulletin, cars of railway revenue freight loaded on lines in Canada in the last days of April numbered 90,056 compared to 99,598 for a like period last year, bringing the month's total to 281,378 cars as compared with 307,745.
Then, of course, the serious weakness in our economy is reflected in the statistics on unemployment in this country. Normally we would have had, last Wednesday or Thursday, a further statistical report on the number of applicants for jobs, on the number of

persons without jobs and seeking work, and that would have been supplemented by the figure given the other day to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) as to the number of persons actually in receipt of unemployment insurance as of the last available date.

I rise again on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. It is, in essence, the same point of order I raised a moment ago. I think it must be clear now, Mr. Speaker, what is the purpose the hon. gentleman is seeking to serve by his speech. First, may I recall the true rule with respect to the raising of grievances on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply. I refer to citation 234 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, at the bottom of page 198 and running over to the top of page 199:
When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament or to ask for the redress of any grievance;
May I draw to your attention the fact that the expression used is "public matter", not "matters" in the plural; it is the redress of *"any grievance" not "grievances", in the one motion. We have a strict rule of debate, namely that when the debate has been launched on a particular grievance the course of debate cannot be diverted to another grievance, thus emphasizing the strict necessity of confining speeches on such matters to a particular grievance or a particular public matter.
But that is not at all the line which the hon. gentleman has been following. At point after point in his remarks this afternoon he has been touching upon matters which have already been debated in this house at the present session and on which debate has been concluded by a resolution of the house. He has mentioned housing. We have had a housing debate on a resolution, where this matter has been concluded. We have had discussions on unemployment and we have had motions on unemployment. The hon. gentleman is talking about unemployment. Let me go back to the debate on the speech from the throne and show what ground the hon. gentleman is now recovering in this shotgun approach of his today. On January 18, as reported at page 64 of Hansard, we find an amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to develop and enunciate clear and consistent policies or to provide full and accurate information, is a major cause of the confusion and uncertainty that prevails about national defence, public finance, agriculture, markets, employment and in other important areas of governmental responsibility.
National Board on Economic Development
Again in the budget debate, as reported at page 2873 of Hansard, the first amendment introduced on April 4 was as follows:
This house regrets that the financial policies of the government will produce a fourth consecutive over-all deficit in a year of "so-called prosperity", while at the same time offering no solution to the problem of rising prices, rising trade deficits, a continued high premium on the Canadian dollar, increased pressure on provinces and municipalities to borrow outside Canada, declining farm income, and high and rising unemployment.
You -will recall, Mr. Speaker, that objection was taken to the breadth of that amendment, in view of the broad and inclusive terms of the amendment to the motion for the address in reply to the speech from the throne on January 18. You permitted an amendment which reduced the number of references but left in those pertaining to high and rising unemployment. We had a similar subamendment on April 4, as found at page 2878 of Hansard.
It is quite obvious that the hon. member is conducting an abuse of the rules of the house by just making a shotgun speech in which he is touching on matter after matter which has already been concluded by a decision of the house at the present session, and is evading the point that has been raised head-on by refusing to state his particular grievance.
With great respect, Mr. Speaker, I say this is a highly irregular procedure. In introducing an amendment or speaking to a grievance on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply it is not open to an hon. member to scatter his shots over a great many subjects. Under the rules he is required to confine himself to a subject or a grievance. He is up against two rules. I say with respect, Mr. Speaker, that he has broken both of them. First of all, he has been trespassing very much on matters that have already been decided by the house at the present session, and in the second place he has not been discussing a matter or a grievance as required by the rules.

When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament or to ask for the redress of any grievance; provided that the discussion-
Note, the "discussion", not just the amendment.
-shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
The debate in such a case is limited by the rules respecting past decisions-
And so on. Now, Mr. Speaker, if due weight is given to that sound and recognized rule, it surely is clear that the discussion on this motion must not relate to any decision of the house made during the current session.
What does the Leader of the Opposition argue here? He says that in 1955 the word "unemployment" was mentioned in the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne; that it was mentioned later on a supply motion, and that the word "employment" was mentioned in the amendment to the motion to resolve the house into committee of ways and means.
Mr. Speaker, if I remember correctly-and of course I have not the books here before me-it was when that second motion was introduced, the amendment to the supply motion, that Mr. Speaker Beaudoin raised the point as to whether the amendment was not so broad as to trespass upon a decision taken by the house on the original amendment to the motion for the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As far as previous cases of amendments being introduced in the same session are concerned, without having before me the full text of the amendments to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred may I say that what was justified there was on the basis that the amendment to the budget asked the house to pass censure on the government for failing to take certain specific measures in


the budget to create employment. Obviously it was thought at that time that there was a difference there.

I think there are no difficulties. Your last words would, I am sure, if strictly interpreted, have to be redefined in the light of citation 234. If there is any repetition of the decision already taken, then I am out of order, but only within that context of the amendment referred to by my hon. friend. It does not in any way, as the Leader of the Opposition indicated, touch the point because no decision has been taken on the matter to which I will ask the house to give attention when I have finished what I have to say.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, there are many kinds of unemployment: Frictional, seasonal unemployment, structural unemployment, technological unemployment, unemployment caused by international trade. At this time we have a right to inquire whether the government at any time has given us a careful indication of the character of seasonal unemployment. Certainly the present level of unemployment in Canada does not represent in its entirety seasonal unemployment. But we have unemployment, and this has to be faced, along with other questions, as the governor of the Bank of Canada has recognized. There are solutions for this problem which have not been taken, or certainly which have not been discussed by the government.
We have been told recently in another place about fraud in our employment service. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Thrasher) indicated that that exists and has pointed out the difficulty of eradicating it. I say to the administration that if that is so, no matter how difficult it is it must be the responsibility of the government of Canada to take steps to see that those situations are corrected.
With respect to technological unemployment, we must recognize that our national employment service must be brought up to


its highest possible point of efficiency. We must see to it that the employers of our country fully use this service, if they are not doing so now; we must see to it, in order to make this service the kind of force which the situation now requires in Canada, that our national employment service officers are adequately remunerated to do this very important job.
We have had no indication from the government as to what steps it is prepared to take in the matter of the proper location of industries, such as is being done in England. Those are considerations which at some time or other, if this problem referred to by the governor of the Bank of Canada and others is going to be met, will have to be dealt with.
Are we satisfied to the extent that seasonal employment is a cause that we are taking every step that should be taken to meet this problem? We were told two years ago that the Department of Labour was undertaking studies in the matter of seasonal unemployment to determine its character, to determine remedies. We have never had those studies, and if rumour is correct those studies are not directed toward a proper appreciation of the problem.
At the present time there are thousands of university students, many of them trained, who could be utilized to assist in this important work, a job that was undertaken in the United States and in Great Britain within the last year and half. There are suggestions for reducing seasonal unemployment. There were suggestions made by the congress of labour in the last bulletin which was issued a few days ago. The bulletin embodies suggestions which we have a right to ask the government to consider and tell us whether it has considered them and what its comments are, because if one can accept the logic of the representations made by the congress of labour, they do provide what seem a priori to be solid contributions and solutions.
What does the Minister of Finance think, for instance? What do the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) think about the suggestions made by that body for lowering interest rates on winter construction? What do they think about the suggestion of grants to induce municipalities to carry out construction in winter rather than in other seasons? What about the suggestion of higher depreciation rates on winter projects? What about winter exemptions on building materials from sales tax? What about subsidies to individuals and to firms, municipalities and provincial governments which undertake to do what the national government has been urging?

Those are matters which are put to us for the first time by way of suggestions. We have the right to know whether these matters are being considered, or is the problem being allowed to run its course, and is the government's approach one of relaxed interest?
This is not going to provide the solution in this very difficult period, as the governor of the Bank of Canada points out. I make the suggestion that not enough consideration has been given to the possibility of a special capital investment program in depressed areas.
We have a situation in this country at the present time where we have an exceedingly high level of unemployment despite our proximity to the business cycle peak. Production is at a high level; there is no denying that. Hon. gentlemen sitting on the ministerial benches may refer to that as an achievement, may refer to that as an indication of prosperity. Alongside that is the anomalous fact that in spite of high production there is great unemployment, unemployment which persisted during this year, in 1959, 1958 and in 1957. Employment has not responded in spite of this increase in productivity. We now have a hard core of unemployment, coupled with repetitive seasonal unemployment of substantial proportions, more in this country, according to figures, than is known in any other country in the western world but one, even if one recognizes the different indices and standards which are applied. Incidentally, it is of interest to know that our D.B.S. standard, plus the number of temporary layoffs, is closer to the international labour office standards than any other.
But this problem is not going to solve itself. This problem is not going to be solved unless this government asserts the kind of leadership represented by the courage and the assessment made by the governor of the Bank of Canada, as I hope to show in examining some of the remarks that he makes.
The national problem of unemployment in Canada is aggravated by regional unemployment. The problem, although national in scope, is largely regional in its severity. Our national manpower is being inefficiently utilized. The nation is being deprived of products which could have been produced if our labour force had been fully employed during this period. To correct this situation would involve cost. This is met by the governor of the Bank of Canada in these memorable words which he used in this speech on May 12. Here is what he had to say:
The cost of unemployment and of measures to promote increased employment are real, and must be borne by someone. There are non-inflationary methods to deal with this, if the people of Canada are prepared to share the cost. Such methods 79951-0-261

must all turn on the same basic principle. In one way or another, those of us who are employed must contribute out of our resources to help share the cost of unemployment and to help create conditions in which greater employment opportunities will be available within Canada. The question of maintaining a viable economic structure in different regions of Canada as well as in different industries within Canada is also one which calls above all for a sharing of burdens and opportunities. The cost that must be shared, the price that must be paid in the short run, in order that we may all be better off in the long run, and in order that we may all remain Canadians in the long run, is not in my opinion a very high price, but obviously it is more likely to be voluntarily accepted and undertaken-
This is what I am seeking to do.
-if we all know and study and face up to the facts, and reach a broad measure of agreement on what we want to achieve and what methods are best calculated to bring about the desired achievement.
I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that the speeches made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in Vancouver and in Winnipeg did not touch on this theme. I say at this time that the Minister of Finance, who now finds this somewhat of a laughing matter, must either accept the conclusions of the governor of the bank or repudiate them and resort to the necessary constitutional practices so that in his service and the service of the nation will be those who share his ideas and the ideas of the government of Canada. My hon. friend has not made one reference in any of his speeches to the problem of unemployment. He completely ignored it in Winnipeg, he completely ignored it in Vancouver, and he passed over it in a very cavalier way in the budget speech he made in the house.

But the governor of the Bank of Canada does not overlook the regional aspects of this problem. He said at page 18 of this speech, and I commend this to the Minister of Finance:
And Canada can only be strong and meaningful in terms of national identity if each of its main economic regions is likewise enabled to develop and maintain a healthy economic structure as the varying circumstances of time and place may require.
Does the Minister of Finance agree with that? Does he recognize now what are the facts that are gradually being exposed? The unemployment problem in the maritime provinces is, of course, a manifestation of the national problem, but here are the figures that are given now and which reflect a seriousness that we do not all appreciate. We now find calculations made which show that in January, February and March 75,000, 83,000 and 85,000 people were without jobs and seeking work in that area. This represents 13.6 per cent, 15.2 per cent and 15.9 per cent of
4140	HOUSE OF
National Board on Economic Development the region's labour force. In the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia the total volume of industrial employment has decreased in absolute terms in the period 1956 to 1959.
Then we find that in the province of Quebec, one of the regions where unemployment is greatest, unemployment in March, 1960 was 12,000 higher than in March of 1958. In that province during January, February and March of this year the number of persons without jobs and seeking work was 192,000, 242,000, and 236,000, representing
11.0	per cent, 13.3 per cent and 13.6 per cent respectively in those three months, people who were unemployed and seeking work.
There are, of course, other areas of unemployment in the country. There are several pockets in relatively prosperous regions. According to the latest figures published in the Windsor Star on Friday last, my own city of Windsor still has some 9,000 persons seeking jobs, and that situation has prevailed in that community on an even higher scale during the past three to four months. One recognizes how fortunate we in this country are to have had developed a scheme of social welfare and economic assistance through social measures without which the purchasing power of these unemployed would be negligible, and without which it would be the obligation of every citizen of this country out of their taxes to maintain body and soul, for these people. Under these social measures all of them are now able to be maintained as a matter of right, although one does not forget that last year there was imposed on the unemployment insurance fund a responsibility that belonged to the nation as a whole.
I asked the Minister of Finance the other day whether or not any loans had been made to the unemployment insurance fund and his reply was in the negative. I will admit that he readily corrected himself the next day and pointed out that the Bank of Canada had lent moneys to the unemployment insurance commission-

-$4 million on April 19, $12 million on April 25 and $3 million on April 29, and the minister also indicated that requests for an additional $19 million had been put forward. I would remind the Minister of Finance, as an indication of the economic situation to which I have been directing my attention, that last year was the first year in the history of Canada that the Bank of Canada or the government of Canada, as my friend wishes, was


called upon to lend any money to the unemployment insurance fund. The minister is about to correct me but that is the fact. Last year was the first time there had to be any bolstering of the fund by the Bank of Canada on the authorization of the investment committee and the Minister of Finance.
When the minister was replying the other day he said that the fund will be in balance in the month of June. I make this statement to the minister. Having in mind that last year some $78 million by way of additional contributions was imposed upon the workers and employees of Canada to bolster the fund, an increase from 25 to 55 per cent on the average without providing any increase in the pattern of benefits, if we are confronted next year with anything like the kind of unemployment we have had this year then it will mean that there will not be enough money in the fund to provide the assistance which has been contracted out to the contributors to the fund. That is a serious situation when we take into account the fact that in December, 1956, the fund amounted to $924 million; on March 31, 1957, $874,574,000; on March 31, 1958, $744,200,000; on March 31, 1959, $499,811,000; and on March 31, 1960, $359,949,000. If these figures, brought up to date with the additional information provided by the government, are not a reflection of the economic weakness that prevails at the present time, then I should like to know what is.
We have put before this government proposals. They have all been passed over by the administration. Included in those proposals, which were never voted upon, never were put forward in the form of motions and let us understand that procedurally, were two which embodied proposals made by this government when its leading members were sitting to the left of Mr. Speaker. The government passed over them. The government has refused to act on them.
We urged the setting up in this house of a parliamentary committee to examine these related problems, but that opportunity was not given to us. Instead one aspect of this problem has been referred to a group of experts to try to find some device, which incidentally would have the effect of creating less embarrassment for the government, as a result of which some satisfactory, acceptable figure of unemployment might be given to the country. We have yet to hear as to the progress made by this group, although time marches on.
But, on the other hand, an opportunity has been given for some group outside to study and report upon the trend in manpower requirements and utilization in Canada, with the object of exploring the

possibilities of maintaining and extending a high level of employment and without restricting the opportunity of that group of reporting upon the growth of the economy and all the other factors influencing employment opportunities, including particularly technological changes and the growth of the Canadian labour force. It is an effrontery to this house that the government should have allowed one of its spokesmen elsewhere to prosecute that kind of study, having denied that right to the representatives of the people, chosen in election, who sit in this house.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker,-this was not touched upon by motion, either-there is a standing committee in this house known as the industrial relations committee. This committee has been organized, one meeting has been called and a chairman has been selected. There has not been one meeting of that committee held since that organizational meeting. As a member of the committee I proposed that we ask the House of Commons to give the committee power to investigate the problem of unemployment. The motion was put and every member sitting behind the treasury benches voted against the proposal.

Nothing has been done since. The committee is set up to work, but is not doing anything. We have been denied the right to use that vehicle to study the most important single domestic problem facing the people of Canada, the problem of unemployment.
The matter does not rest there. The congress of labour, through its president, in the month of January suggested at a board of trade meeting in Toronto that the time had come when government, industry and labour should confer together on problems of common interest. I asked the Minister of Labour several times if he would convoke such a conference. I was always able to receive from the minister polite replies, but the government never met the suggestion. I put this question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), and it will be found on page 616 of Hansard for February 2, 1960, early in the session:
The Prime Minister will recall that I asked this question myself ten days ago. Will the Prime Minister now say whether or not the government has given consideration to this proposal made by the president of the congress of labour three weeks ago when he spoke to the board of trade meeting in Toronto?
The Prime Minister answered:
The answer is no.
That was with regard to a matter, I say again, which touches the most important single domestic problem in our country. We have urged repeatedly, not by way of a motion, on the government and on the Minister of Labour in particular to call such a conference, but without any success. I was pleased but astonished when on Friday last in reading the Ottawa Citizen I noticed a report of a speech made by the Minister of Labour. Here is the speech as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 20, and the heading is, "Starr Asks Three-Way Market Bid":
Gananoque, CP: Labour Minister Starr Thursday night called on labour, management and government to consult together to maintain a competitive position for Canada in world trade.
I do not know whether or not that is an announcement of policy. I hope the Minister of Labour secured authorization to say that. We certainly will back him up because that is something we have been contending for and urging upon the Prime Minister and others, something that labour itself has been

National Board on Economic Development asking, that the national chamber of commerce has been asking. Surely the Minister of Labour will now take advantage of his own proposal which confirms what we have been urging all through this session, so that at long last these questions might be put on a co-operative basis in order to try to find some procedural way of determining what steps should be taken to meet the serious problems that confront us, of which unemployment is but one.
The minister referred to the competitive position of Canada and that obviously is a very important matter. No decision can be taken which adversely affects the income position of labour without giving labour an opportunity of discussing its position with government and with industry. Nothing but good can come out of this suggestion. I should like to say that the Leader of the Opposition suggested in 1958, when speaking about the same problem of unemployment and the indications of a recession, the establishment of an advisory board with representatives from labour, industry, agriculture and the univer-problems of production and employment.
I now, as spokesman in this instance for my party, with the Leader of the Opposition sitting by and with whom I have discussed this matter as I have with my colleagues, urge the government to set up such a board on economic development to assist the government in prosecuting the problems which have been underlined by the governor of the Bank of Canada and which, in some instances, have not been recognized by the government of the day. That proposal was consistent with the suggestion made in 1957 by the Gordon commission which reported as follows:
We believe it might be helpful if a body of experts were established (along the lines of the council of economics advisers to the President of the United States), whose function it would be to inform the government of changes which might be thought desirable in economic policy in order to ensure a high level of employment without inflation.
Then we have supporting the position we are taking the recommendation made by the mayors of Canada at their last meeting which was held in Chicago. In the London Free Press of May 12 an article headed "Overwhelming Support Given by Delegates" reads in part as follows:
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities yesterday called upon the federal government to appoint an impartial board of inquiry or royal commission to investigate unemployment in Canada.

Although we have our difficulties and problems, let us not forget that we are capable of providing Canadians in all parts of Canada with a way of life which even in economic terms need be second only to that of the richest and most powerful nation in the world, and in Canadian eyes and taking account of non-material values as well, second to none. We do not have to choose between poverty-stricken independence and some form of economic colonialism, either for Canada as a whole or for any of the regions of Canada. If we put Canadianism in the forefront of our economic and social thinking, and recognize each other as fellow Canadians, if we co-operate and share, we can be both independent and wealthy, even as the world measures wealth. If we are sufficiently determined to pay our own way and make our own place in the world, all Canadians in every part of Canada can achieve productive employment, with an ever-widening range of modern industrial and scientific occupations available to them, and can maintain a standard of living and way of life which in the sum of all its aspects will be capable of satisfying the highest aspirations of the human spirit.
Those are the words that should be uttered by a Prime Minister or by a Minister of Finance if they are prepared seriously to acknowledge the prognosis referred to by men who are regarded as experts in this field, some of whom are now serving the government and the people of Canada in our public service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intended that of course not as a reflection on Your Honour but as a reflection on the minister who did seek to debate the substance of what I have said. Whether he accepts what I say is a matter for argument;


but to suggest that it is irrelevant is the very subject of the present procedural discussion before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: The hon. member is not allowed to reflect on another hon. member.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
The minister
keeps talking about a grievance. We are not raising a grievance. The hon. member has apparently not understood what the citation from Beauchesne is intended to convey. Citation 234, as I as well as the minister have already quoted several times, provides:
When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament or to ask for the redress of any grievance-
That is the alternative.
There is before the house an amendment which calls upon the government to give consideration to certain matters, but we are not proposing ourselves to set up a committee. We have no power to set up a committee and consequently no expenditure is involved under this particular amendment. All we are asking the government to do is to consider the immediate setting up of a national advisory board, et cetera. If the government decides it will come in with a resolution, it will make the proposal for the expenditure of money. This is merely a request in the form of an amendment in the time-honoured manner of asking the government to give consideration to a procedure which we believe would be one way by which the problems discussed in my statement could be considered for their validity or otherwise.
It is clear that what Speaker Beaudoin was referring to was something that involved a matter which had already been attended to by way of decision. The amendment now before the house is something that has not been proposed formally in this house this session. As far as I know, I am not aware of its having been proposed at any time in parliament. It has been proposed now for the first time, and the substance of the amendment is the setting up of machinery to discuss a number of matters, namely to set up a national advisory 'board on economic development and automation with representatives of government, and so on. But I repeat, the substance of the motion is to set up such a body.
The hon. minister speaking on the amendment says that this point has already been dealt with. With great respect I would point out to Your Honour that in the amendment moved on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the word "employment" was mentioned as one of five fields about which confusion and uncertainty prevailed. It was

not the substance of the motion. There has been no decision in this house this session on the question of unemployment. But that is not the substance of my amendment. My amendment does not deal with the question of unemployment as such; it deals with the setting up of a committee to study a number of problems of which unemployment is one. The words "high and rising unemployment" were used in the budget amendment as one of four problems for which the budget offered no solution. But the very language of that amendment is clear. It is: "This house regrets that the financial policies of the government will produce a fourth consecutive over-all deficit in a year of so-called prosperity". The amendment was an expression of regret, at the same time offering no solution to the problem of rising prices, rising trade deficits, and so on. So that if we accept, as I think Your Honour will on consideration, that this particular amendment is one that deals with the setting up of an advisory committee, there can be no doubt about the validity of the amendment and that it is in order.
As I indicated, citation 234 (1) sets forth what may be discussed on such a motion. The main question arising from this citation is whether the amendment now being proposed relates to any decision of the house during the current session. That is the procedural point which will interest Your Honour.
In this connection I would like to go further than the hon. minister. I would like to examine the authorities to show how fallacious is the position he has taken. I refer Your Honour to citation 191 (3) of Beauchesne, which reads as follows:
The question Is the subject matter of the motion, and on the merits of that subject matter the House has to give a decision either unanimously or by the majority of the members present. The Speaker proposes the question in the words of the mover. When the motion has been seconded it merges in the question which is read by the Speaker, after which the house is in possession of the question and must dispose of it. Every question when agreed to assumes the form either of an order or a resolution of the house. By its orders the house directs its committees, its members, its officers, the order of its own proceedings and the acts of all persons they concern; by its resolutions the house declares its own opinions and purposes.
It must be noted that the opinions and purposes which it declares are not ones involving any expenditure of money. They are merely calling upon the administration to give consideration to certain matters.
Then there is citation 194:
A motion or amendment cannot be brought forward which is the same in substance as a question which has already been decided, because a proposition being once submitted and carried in the affirmative or negative cannot be questioned again but must stand as the judgment of the house. This rule applies to the decision taken on amendments
National Board on Economic Development
to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. A question once put cannot be altered by the member moving it, without the consent of the house. The reconsideration of a question already decided is not allowed under British parliamentary practice, but it prevails in many public bodies and societies. A resolution may however be rescinded, i.e. it may be made void and of no effect. A question once put cannot be altered by the member moving it, without the consent of the house.
These citations together clarify the meaning of the word "question". The main consideration is the substance of the amendment and not its appendices, or matters which are merely incidental to it. One could have left out any reference to a high and stable level of income and employment without in any way affecting the substance of the motion. One could certainly have left out the word "employment" without in any way affecting the substance.
It is apparent that at no time in the current session has this house reached a decision on setting up a board of the kind proposed. To deny this amendment would be to take away from the opposition the right to seek a decision on this matter by an amendment of this character. The Minister of Finance, in the budget debate, attacking the validity of our amendment, quoted citation 148(1) of Beauchesne which reads in part:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded-
The hon. gentleman made reference to that, but that does not mean anything. What is significant is this: what do we mean by the word "concluded"? The question is: when is a debate concluded? The answer to that is provided in citation 120 which states that a debate is concluded when a decision is reached by the house. I will read citation 120 because it surely will convince Your Honour, if that is now required, as to the soundness of the position which we have taken. Citation 120 reads as follows:
The proceedings between the rising of a member to move a motion and the ascertainment by the chair of the decision of the house constitute a debate, and this process affords an opportunity for, and usually involves, discussion, although a decision may be reached without discussion. The interval between the proposing and the putting of the question, which is usually used for discussion, gives an opportunity tor further proceedings such as the moving of an amendment; and this may give rise to a subsidiary debate, with its own question and decision, within the principal debate.
And then:
Debate arises when a question has been proposed by the Speaker and before it has been fully put. A question is fully put when the Speaker has taken the voices of the ayes and the noes.
Thus it should be stressed that the substance of the amendment before the house is the creation of a board to develop economic
4146	HOUSE OF
National Board on Economic Development policies, and though unemployment and income are mentioned, these are incidental references within the amendment and do not constitute its substance. For this simple reason this matter, under our rules and under the citations to which I have referred, does not come within the mischief of the word "conclude".
I submit these representations to Your Honour confident in the belief that you will recognize their validity. They are founded on precedent and they are supported by our practice.

Has the hon. member any comment to make on that, because I would consider this to be a repetition of that debate, on which a conclusion was reached by a decision to negative the amendment, and would not be in accordance with the proper practice of the house.

speechtext:
I can only say to Your Honour in reply as to the view you take to the amendment to which allusion has just been made, that I can only, with respect, take issue with Your Honour, because I believe that in the amendment the reference to unemployment was incidental. However, Your Honour apparently takes another view, a view which I had hoped it would be possible to shake. I can only state that I believe the very language of that amendment indicates that it was incidental. But whether or not it was incidental then, the point is that it is clearly incidental now. I believe it was incidental in both cases. The substance of the motion before the house is:
This house recommends for the consideration of the government the immediate setting up of a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives of governments, industry, labour, agriculture and universities, for the purpose of developing economic policies-

speechtext: Hon. gentlemen opposite say, "no". That is a matter for the Speaker, and I am sure none of them wishes to usurp that function.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
If I may say one word on the question which you have raised, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the closest precedent both


in time and in nature is that to which I have already referred-the occasion in the session of 1955. In that session, as has already been pointed out, the hon. member for Dufferin moved an amendment to the address in which he regretted on behalf of the opposition that the government had failed to take or recommend the necessary measures-and then there is a list of six fields, of which the second is unemployment. The words were, in fact:
(b) to solve the urgent problem of unemployment.
In the debate which took place at that time the subject of unemployment was brought in, but all the other matters referred to in those various other fields were also discussed. That did not prevent, nor did the government of the day seek to prevent, the opposition moving an amendment on going into supply which again dealt specifically with one of these matters, namely unemployment, though in a somewhat different form, because that motion read:
That the government should immediately give consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency of unemployment.
That motion was accepted. It was debated, and it was decided, and it seems to me that if such a situation prevailed at that time this particular motion is surely in order, because it is not as closely related as those two motions were in 1955; it is not as closely related to any previous discussion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
Perhaps I could shorten this discussion by indicating my views on some of the points which have been raised, and the remaining difficulties. On the point the minister makes about the amendment involving the expenditure of money, I think the general approach, or the formula, by which the matter is recommended to the government is sufficient answer. It is that the house recommends for the consideration of the government. That is the form which has been used in many of our motions by private members. If it is accepted it does not commit the government; it does not commit the government to spend money. It asks the government only to consider setting up a committee, to give expression to it. In other words, the decision of the house does not bind the government to set up a committee, it only puts the government under an obligation to give consideration to setting up the committee.
On the question of whether this is a grievance or not, I should like to refer hon. members to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, which defines this procedure in terms which I think are worthy of consideration. I refer to page 419:
The order of the day for the house to go into committee of supply having been read, the Speaker will put the question-"that I do now leave the

chair''. The same question is always put whenever the house is to go into committee of supply, in order to afford an opportunity to members to propose amendments. On this point it is observed by an eminent authority that the ancient constitutional doctrine that the redress of grievances is to be considered before the granting of supplies, is now represented by the practice of permitting every description of amendment to be moved on the question for the Speaker leaving the chair, before going into committee of supply or ways and means.
"Every description of amendment"; there was no right of parliament broader than that of raising grievances before voting supply and, as Bourinot points out by reference to this authority, that right is preserved in our supply motions. I continue with the citation:
Upon other orders of the day, such amendments must be relevant, but here they are permitted to relate to every question upon which a member may desire to offer a motion. The same practice is now followed very extensively in the Canadian commons.
I have no hesitation in coming to the conclusion that a resolution recommending to the government that it consider setting up a committee, something which it has not done, is a grievance within the very broad terms of grievances, which include anything within the administrative power of the government, about which the commons can complain in the course of the process of granting supply.
The other point is the difficult one, to my mind, whether we are opening ourselves to repetition of debate that has been concluded by a vote. That difficulty arises not out of the recommendation for the setting up of this committee or in anything it says but in the words:
-for the purpose of developing economic policies-
Then, it goes on:
-designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment.
I cannot help but recall the words of the amendment to the budget resolution, which dealt with the financial policies of the government with respect to employment. Here we come to economic policies with respect to employment. While "economic" is perhaps a broader word and is more inclusive than the financial policies of the government, yet economic policies might be those of private industry and other agencies. This is the problem that remains and if, before I come to a decision, the minister or others would like to address themselves to that point briefly, I would be grateful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
Thank you. I would like to say a further word about it, to put before you as directly as I can the position in which hon. members would find themselves if this were ruled to be in order.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) cannot just conveniently drop words 79951-0-262
National Board on Economic Development from his motion and ask you to consider the motion at this point as if they were not in, because these are the principal words of the motion. He asks the house to recommend that the government set up a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives from various sources. These are the words:
-for the purpose of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment.
This is the whole purpose for which he asks that consideration be given to the setting up of a board. What are the policies? Those are policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment. No hon. member in this house can hope to discuss this question-I think this is the nub and essence of the whole question now submitted to you for decision-no hon. member can discuss this motion without going directly into the questions pertaining broadly to the achievement of a high and stable level of income and employment. This is precisely the question that was under debate in the budget debate. This is precisely the question that was raised by the amendment introduced by the opposition on April 4. We had such a debate back at the end of January and through February on the supplementary estimates, when we had an eight-day discussion on unemployment in this country and all manner of methods of coping with unemployment or aiding in reducing it. Yet we are now asked to go back and review that question all over again; we are asked now to review the whole question that was raised directly in the budget debate and do that all over again, because we are told this narrows the discussion down to a particular point.
That particular point can only be fairly judged in any approach to it by any hon. member in this house in relation to the broader question, and that broader question has been directly raised in debate this session not once, but I am sure at least twice, on the occasions I have mentioned. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, my submission is that that is the test and, having regard to the fact that the hon. member has attempted to justify the amendment and the grievance that it is supposed to deal with on the basis that it is assisting in achieving a high and stable level of income and employment, I say that these words bring him completely within the scope of those earlier motions.
It is not a matter of words only, although the words bring the amendment clearly within that scope, but it is the substance as well. The citation from Beauchesne which was quoted emphasizes the matter of substance. If this amendment were allowed to stand we would embark now on another

National Board on Economic Development debate on unemployment, the same question as has already been debated frequently this session.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION

Mr. Speaker, perhaps you could deal with the precedent which I mentioned. It seems to me to bear very directly on this issue.
So far as the argument of my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, is concerned, it really would amount to this if it were accepted, that because we talked about national income and unemployment six weeks, or two weeks ago we should not be permitted to talk about it during the rest of this session, no matter how conditions may have changed and no matter how necessary it may be for the government to take steps to meet those changed conditions. This is the logical inference to be drawn from my hon. friend's argument.
It is some weeks since we talked about unemployment in the budget. Since that time there have been changes in the situation. In our view the situation has perhaps deteriorated to the point where we think it more important now to set up machinery to deal with it than it was even then.
If this motion were in a form merely to advise the government to consider the setting up of a board in the terms in which they appear to be prescribed, a national advisory board on economic development and automation; if the motion stopped there with the names of its members, is it suggested by my hon. friend that in discussing the work of this board we should not be permitted to say what it might do in respect of income and employment? If he takes that position, it is absurd. If he does not take that position, surely by mentioning employment and a stable level of income we are not to be precluded from talking about them when if they were omitted we could talk about them. That is the situation as it appears to me.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION

I think the essential purpose expressed in the proposed amendment is the consideration of "a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives of governments, industry, labour, agriculture and universities". In other words, it is not a purely governmental body but an advisory board "for the purpose of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment".
I think the amendment is capable of the interpretation that the purposes of the proposed board are in general the maintenance of a high level of economic activity in the country. Unemployment is not mentioned although it is the converse of employment, and undoubtedly there is a risk that one matter which has been decided, the effect of the financial policies of the government with respect to unemployment, would be revived and an attempt made to debate it. But that was a narrow amendment, one which is an illustration of a different principle and having to do with the financial policy of the government rather than an advisory board. As I am in considerable doubt I think I should give the benefit to the proposer of the amendment with the caution that I will not regard it as opening the door to a debate on the financial policies of the government with

respect to unemployment, which subject has been dealt with as an amendment to the budget motion.
