subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
I am not going to repeat what I said a few minutes ago, but merely emphasize that what I have to say on this amendment is related only to that aspect of it which applies to the recommendation that the government consider the immediate setting up of a national advisory board on development and automation. I feel that automation is one of the very serious and irrevocable developments in our economy to which sufficient attention has not been paid in so far as planning is concerned in connection with its impact and its implications.
Undoubtedly the problem has been well known for some considerable time. I should like to draw the attention of the house to a short quotation from a speech. I just want to quote the concluding paragraph because I think it is of interest. It reads:
When we encounter problems of adjustment arising out of a national endeavour to reap the benefits that advancing technology, including automation, brings us, let us remember that most of these can be overcome by patient application, good will, and the co-operation of all sectors of our economy. Let us see such problems in their proper perspective, and let us remember that their solution is helping Canadians in facing up to a great challenge. And that is to replace:
The hunger for power and the hunger of poverty with the benefits of peace and the benefits of progress.

This is a quotation from a speech that was made on March 23, 1956, by Mr. J. H. Dickey, parliamentary assistant to the minister of defence production, to the society for the advancement of management in Montreal. At least there was one Liberal in an official capacity in 1956 who recognized the advance of automation and who recognized that something should be done about it. But at that time the previous government did nothing about it. We are very glad of their interest now. It is also unfortunate that, at least to the best of my knowledge, no specific study or action is being taken by the present government to consider all the problems of automation as it is growing now, and undoubtedly as we will have it in the not too distant future.
Over the years the intensity of this problem has been forcibly brought home, or should have been brought home, to governments and to all parties, irrespective of whether they are in government or in opposition. I was most interested in reading the report of the Director-General of the International Labour Office on automation and other technological developments. This report was made in 1957 and made it exceptionally clear that those interested in the welfare of the country, the welfare of the economy and the problems that arise because of technological advances, should be doing something about these things. I just want to quote a couple of sentences. He said:
There is no doubt that we have entered a new technological era. Automation and atomic energy, unfolding simultaneously, are already causing drastic changes in the world of industry and labour...
Automation, atomic energy and other technological changes are dominating the labour and social scene in more and more of the older industrial countries and are a key factor in the development of the newly industrializing countries. They pose serious problems of economic and social adjustment for our industrial society and throw down a challenge to our whole civilization. True, many of these problems are not new. They arose in earlier stages of industrialization. Today, however, they seem to take on a more dramatic and a more drastic form.
The point I want to make is that we have had indications in the past as to the importance of this question of automation, and nothing has been done. It is for this reason I believe the hon. member for Essex East has done a great service to this House of Commons, and to the people of this country, in raising the issue as he has today through the medium of this amendment which suggests that the government do something about it. Apparently, although it may not be a tactic that is generally recognized as being acceptable, you have to keep pounding away at and hounding the government to try to get them to do the things which it seems so obvious they should be doing.

This matter has been drawn to the attention of the present government time after time, and yet we do not see any action. The Canadian Labour Congress in its memorandum to the government of Canada on January 28 requested a continued study of the effects of automation and the development of a program of training and retraining and other measures to assist in the re-establishment of workers displaced by automation and technological changes generally. Then, too, we have the submission to this government of the national legislative committee of the international railway brotherhoods, dated February 2, 1960. They stated:
May we urge that at this session of parliament a committee of the House of Commons be established to investigate and report on the effects of technological changes and automation.
Not as a direct submission to the government-but I know that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) must follow what is said by union leaders-we have the report of Larry Sefton, director of the united steelworkers of America at their national policy conference held in Montreal on April 21 and 22, of this year, dealing with this question of automation, its effects now and its probable effects on labour in the future. I know there are those people who think that labour is not prepared to accept progress, new technological developments and automation. That is why I think it is well worth while to draw to the attention of the house in connection with this matter the words of Larry Sefton in the statement I have just mentioned in which he states as follows:
Workers and unions should not try to block technological progress, but a company or industry should be compelled to give consideration to human and social factors when it contemplates relocation of its operations. In many ways, unions can fill the breach with imaginative and constructive collective bargaining programs. These programs will not interfere with or question management's decision to relocate. They will, however, compel management to weigh the human costs involved in such moves, and not merely unload the burden on the workers and the communities.
In dealing with automation from the viewpoint of the worker-and he is the one who is really affected-the question naturally arises as to how labour is affected and why the workers are worrying so much about growing automation in our country of Canada.
I will say that for the workers there are five big questions about automation. First, what is it? Second, what can it do? Third, how far will it go? Fourth, how fast will it come about? Fifth, what will it do to present jobs? Those are questions that are in the minds of the workers and they are questions to which the workers and the trade unions are entitled to an answer.

The answer can come only either through the direct co-operation of industry, labour and government or indirectly through that co-operation through the medium of the procedure which is outlined by the hon. member for Essex East in the course of his amendment which we are now discussing. Surely we recognize the fact-or at least I hope so-that technological advance-such as that represented by chemurgy and automation-is not the brain child of one person, a thousand persons, a million persons or one country. It is the sum total of the understanding, the progress, the research and the inventiveness of all mankind. That being so, all must benefit.
That also is basically what the trade union leaders and the working people of our country are asking. They are asking that the government of this country make certain that the benefits of scientific advance are distributed equitably throughout all society in Canada. They are saying-as does this amendment-that management, labour and government must sit down together and do a great deal of planning.
It should have been started a long time ago but what is the use of recrimination and what is the use of going back and doing too much condemnation and damning? We cannot alter what has happened in the past. We must start from today. I think the need for it was clearly put even back in 1956 by the labour research department of the Canadian congress of labour. I just want to quote from their February issue of that year in which they state as follows:
The problem of automation and employment in Canada can be solved. But it won't solve itself. Automation can give all of us more leisure without throwing any of us permanently out of work. It can give us a much higher standard of living. But it won't do either unless we act to make sure that it does.
It can make goods cheaper; but only if monopolies don't get in the way.
It can shorten hours; but only if employers don't decide that it's simpler and cheaper for them, individually at any rate, to lay people off rather than to spread work.
It can give us much higher wages, but only if management and investors don't collar a lion's share of the increased productivity.
It can benefit us in the long run; but only if we see to it that it benefits us in the series of short runs which make up the long run.
I believe those are sensible words and fair ones. But somebody must initiate the studies and the planning. Then, of course, when that is done there must be an initiating body in order to see that the benefits which accrue through scientific advance are equitably divided amongst all society. To me, at any rate, it appears that the only body that can initiate the planning and the action is the national government of the country. Hence
4152	HOUSE OF
National Board on Economic Development I am saying these few words and commenting on some of the various publications on this matter, in the hope that the seriousness of the problem of automation and the recognition of how directly it is going to affect all the working men and women of this country will result in our doing something about the problem now in the way of planning and action.
I believe that the basic principle was very well put by Norbert Wiener, professor of mathematics at Massachussetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, when he pointed out as follows:
We must always exert the full strength of our imagination to examine where the full use of our new modalities may lead us.
That is what we in this group urge that we do here, irrespective of party, or whether we sit on the government side or the opposition side, namely recognize the problem or the challenge. I am going to conclude with this thought because I want to say only a few words on it. It depends to a great extent on those who are now members of the House of Commons and on the party which now forms the government whether automation is going to be a curse or a blessing. A great responsibility rests on our shoulders in answering that question. It can be answered. The answer lies in how well we who have been elected to legislative office are prepared both to face up to and to pick up the challenge.
As I say, this matter has come to the attention of governments and parties over the years. We have never picked it up yet, but the time is now here when we have to pick it up because automation is no longer in the future, it is here. It is facing the workers, it is facing the unions, it is facing industry, and on a competitive basis. So I say let us decide by our thinking and our action on behalf of the people of Canada as their legislators whether automation will be a curse or a blessing. One way to give that answer is in this house, either today or tomorrow, by supporting an amendment which says that the government should consider following a certain procedure in order that proper studies can be given to these questions and recommendations made for the advice and consideration of the government.

These are some of the suggestions they made at that time as to what in their opinion would create a high level of employment:
Other possible employment stimulators are tax cuts, bigger income tax exemptions, higher social security payments, more aid to farmers, more aid to underdeveloped countries.
Generally speaking, when I have heard representations of this kind made my first reaction has been to say: That is all very well, but if you want the government to spend more money and if you want lower taxes, it is utterly impossible. But in making those statements to the labour organizations I entirely underestimated the capabilities of our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who, I might say is, in my opinion, the best Minister of Finance we have ever had in this country or are ever likely to have.

To refresh my memory on this the other day I obtained a copy of the T-l short form income tax return for 1956 and for 1959, and I shall just pick out one or two examples at random to show that notwithstanding those tremendous payments that have been made by the federal government to the provinces, notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Finance has been able to present a balanced budget this year and in fact forecast a slight surplus, we were able at the same time to enjoy tax cuts. National Board on Economic Development
It is evident that a high and stable level of employment and healthy economic position cannot be achieved by the implementation of the policies of the present government. We therefore have every reason and every right to suggest to the government the setting up of a national advisory board on economic development and automation. The government has failed so far to listen to the suggestions which have emanated from this side of the house in the last few months, and as we have a strong desire to reduce unemployment to a minimum we are placing before the government a new suggestion which we feel could provide badly needed guidance and advice to enable the government to cope with this national problem.
In the few minutes at my disposal I should like to deal more specifically with the amendment as it affects the Atlantic provinces. This is an area, a section of the country which, unlike many others, is not blessed with the kind of natural resources that spurt out of the ground and produce large incomes without too much imaginative initiation or without too risky capital investment. The urgent need for getting together the representatives of industry, labour, agriculture and the universities is more evident in the Atlantic provinces than in any other areas of Canada. In fact, a step in that direction was taken a few years ago with the formation of the Atlantic provinces economic council, and the results of co-operation with that organization are already being felt in some sections of the Atlantic provinces. In no other section of this country today is there a more urgent need for this than in the Atlantic provinces. Our 105,000 unplaced applicants, as of April 30 of this year, reaffirm the fact that our percentage of 14.5 per cent of our labour force seeking jobs remains close to 50 per cent above the national average and almost 85 per cent above the Ontario average.
I know that I would be called out of order if I chose to discuss, in all its detail, the unfortunate unemployment situation in the Atlantic provinces. speechtext: They are being lost now by the policies of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: What are the facts in respect of the economy of this country? In the first place labour income in this country is at a record high. Last month, for the first time in the history of this country, we passed the $75 weekly average of labour income in the country.

speechtext: So has unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: Industrial expansion has continued at unprecedented rates; steel mills were at 104 per cent capacity in March; production was up all along the line. What does the Canadian Statistical Review say on page 19 of the 1959 supplement? It shows that in 1954, those buoyant days of Liberal rule- 1954 is the year they always point to; the hon. member for Essex East mentioned that date this afternoon-industrial production stood at 128.5. This was in the buoyant days of Liberal rule. In March, 1960, the latest available figure, it stood at 169.3, a gain of nearly 41 points.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: You said that this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
Let us look at employment. In manufacturing, in 1959 there were 172,000 more Canadians at work than in 1954; 50,000 more in transportation; 110,000 more at work at construction; 315,000 more at work in service industries and 118,000 more working in trade. There has been a decline in farm labour, but this is due to two things: first, increasing mechanization of farms and, second, the movement of people from farm work to more highly paid industrial jobs. This transition, Mr. Speaker, has been going on since the second world war. There is nothing new in it. Economists have been pointing this out for many years and we get these reports from them continually.
The simple fact of the matter is that this is one of the symptoms of an economy in a state of transition. In the final report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, the following appears:
The record of growth reflects the emergence of this country as an increasingly versatile, skilled and rich industrial nation.
This change-over has been taking place at a rate unparalleled in any modern country,


with the exception perhaps of Japan. Even in Japan problems of technological change and automation are becoming increasingly difficult and, from the reports we get, even in the Soviet union.
What would this committee come up with? Would it come up with something similar to what the committee dealing with the Atlantic provinces came up with?

My department is currently studying the effects of automation, and we have already made a survey touching on the electrical industry, the heavy machinery industry, the household appliance industry and the automobile industry. The committee established by the department is composed of labour representatives among others, and they are studying these things. You have to be an expert. The board suggested in this amendment could not study automation. How would you be able to pick for the personnel of such a board people who would know anything about automation? Automation needs to be studied by experts and that is what we have in the department. That is exactly how we are proceeding in an endeavour to find out what is happening in the field of automation and how it affects labour and manpower. To illustrate how difficult a job this is, I might say that it takes from six months to a year to conduct an on the spot survey in only one industry.
To come back to the amendment, Mr. Speaker, the problems we have to face are not problems that can be solved by any committee. They are problems that must be met by the government which was elected to do the job and which showed in 1958 that it could meet these problems. I do not feel too disappointed when I hear the hon. member for Essex East and others endeavouring to find loopholes whereby they can gain favour in the eyes of the people of the country. speechtext: My embarrassment, Mr. Speaker, arises from the fact that you apparently have not resumed your seat after calling it ten o'clock in order to permit me to ask what the business of the house will be for Wednesday of this week.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The business for this week will be found on page 4072 of Hansard but I now suggest a change for Wednesday due to certain circumstances beyond our control. For one thing, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs with regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act will be postponed at the request of the members of the standing committee on veterans affairs, and the order of business for Wednesday will run this way: Item No. 8 on today's order paper, the resolution with regard to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, followed by the second reading of Bill No. S-27, an act to control and regulate the sale of feeds, followed by the budget resolutions.

Business of the House Mr. Mcllrailh: As I understand it, it was indicated on page 4072 that consideration of the budget resolutions will precede the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That was the original intention, but there is a funeral ceremony that a number of hon. members are attending on the morning of Wednesday. They will be back late on Wednesday afternoon. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is concerned, and
he will be back in time to proceed with budget resolutions, though later than anticipated.
So that the order will now be the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and the act to control and regulate the sale of feeds and then the budget resolutions for Wednesday.
